passage: Last spring I nearly bought a used scooter from Wasim, a mechanic two streets from my PG. "Eighty-five thousand, madam, almost new," he said, patting the seat. My first thought was that seventy-five would be a steal. Then I caught myself. Why seventy-five? Only because he'd said eighty-five. So I asked myself a different question: if I had walked in and seen this scooter with no price on it, what would I think it was worth? I honestly didn't know. That evening I checked two resale listings for the same model and year, and asked my cousin, who sells bikes in Nagpur. All three said around sixty. I offered sixty-two. Wasim grumbled, then agreed. I'm Devika, and I still ride it.

qa.q: How much did Wasim first ask for the scooter?
qa.a: Wasim asked for eighty-five thousand.

qa.q: Why did Devika stop herself after thinking seventy-five would be a steal?
qa.a: She noticed that seventy-five only felt fair because Wasim had said eighty-five, and she didn't want his number deciding the price for her.

qa.q: Which of Devika's steps could someone copy when a seller names a price?
qa.a: Ask what the item would be worth with no price on it, then get two or three separate comparisons, like listings and someone in the trade, before making an offer.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Devika's offer of sixty-two?
qa.a: Wasim probably grumbled because the high opening didn't work this time, but an offer backed by the market was hard to argue with.

grounding: Shows a young woman setting aside a seller's first price by imagining the scooter unpriced and gathering three independent comparisons before offering.

passage:
Supervisor's note, purchase team, Friday. Written by Arnab.
Kalyani handled her first laptop order for the new interns this week. The supplier opened with one lakh ten thousand per unit and called it a "special rate". I expected her to bargain down from there, as most new staff do. Instead she said she would reply by Monday. In her working file I later saw a line: "What would I pay if I'd never heard 1.1?" Under it she had three separate quotes: a second supplier, the government purchase portal price, and our own order from last year. All sat near eighty-two thousand. She went back with eighty-three and her reasons. The deal closed at eighty-four. Next step: I have asked her to show the method at the team meeting.

qa.q: What rate did the supplier call a "special rate"?
qa.a: The supplier called one lakh ten thousand per unit a special rate.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani ask for time until Monday instead of bargaining at once?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to have felt wary of the supplier's "special rate" and wanted to step away from that figure so it wouldn't set her starting point. Asking for time let her calmly find out what the laptops were really worth first.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's three comparisons useful?
qa.a: They came from separate sources, another supplier, a public purchase price and last year's order, so none of them was pulled by the supplier's opening number.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Kalyani's approach?
qa.a: Arnab expected her to bargain down from the opening like most new staff, and is impressed enough to ask her to teach the method to the team.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking what she would pay without the supplier's first figure and collecting three independent comparisons before deciding.

passage:
Thursday night
Omkar's studio quoted ₹90,000 for Tai's engagement photos. My first reaction: okay, maybe we can get it to 75. Then I stopped. Would I have guessed 75 if nobody had said 90? No idea! So I did the boring thing. Called two other photographers that Tai's friends had used: 45 and 55 for the same hours. Also asked Tushar, who shoots weddings in Nashik, what's normal. He said 50 is fair and 90 is "big-hotel pricing". Told Aai. She laughed and said I'm the only daughter who does homework for a party. Booked the 55 one; her candid shots are lovely. Weird how 75 felt cheap this morning.
Charu

qa.q: What did the two other photographers charge for the same hours?
qa.a: They charged 45 and 55 for the same hours.

qa.q: Why did Charu stop after thinking of 75?
qa.a: She realised 75 only came to mind because Omkar's studio had said 90 first, and she wanted to know the fair price without that number in her head.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who gets a high first quote, based on Charu's day?
qa.a: Pause before countering, ask what you would guess with no quote at all, and collect two or three separate prices or opinions, like Charu's calls and Tushar's view, before deciding. 👍

qa.q: How might Omkar's studio see losing the booking?
qa.a: The studio may be surprised, since a high opening usually leads to bargaining near it; this time the customer came back with outside prices and went elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing that her counter-offer was pulled by the first quote, then resetting by gathering independent prices before booking.

passage:
(Tanuja, on the bus home from the interview)
Tanuja: they offered 22k a month for the physics batches
Zeenat: ooh! taking it?
Tanuja: my first thought was ask for 25. then i caught myself
Tanuja: 25 only feels right bc they said 22
Zeenat: meaning?
Tanuja: if nobody had said any number, what would i ask? no idea honestly
Tanuja: so i'm asking around first
Tanuja: messaged 3 people. Rukhsar at the other centre gets 30. Deepti's institute pays 28 for 2 batches. the govt tuition scheme is 26 plus travel
Zeenat: so 22 is low 😮
Tanuja: yep. i'll ask for 30 and explain the batch sizes
Zeenat: proud of you, madam 😄
Tanuja: also scared lol. but it's my number now, not theirs

qa.q: How much does Rukhsar get at the other centre?
qa.a: Rukhsar at the other centre gets 30.

qa.q: Why does Tanuja say it's "my number now, not theirs"?
qa.a: She has built her figure from three outside comparisons, so she feels it rests on real information instead of on the 22 they said first. That gives her confidence even though she is still scared.

qa.q: What was the key moment that changed how Tanuja approached the offer?
qa.a: When she noticed 25 only felt right because they said 22, and asked what she would judge with no number at all. That led her to gather comparisons before answering.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see Tanuja by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Zeenat seems impressed and proud, calling her "madam," and may also learn to ask around before accepting a first figure.

grounding: A young woman notices a salary offer is steering her, asks what she would judge without it, and collects three independent comparisons.

passage: At the Thursday haat in Pipariya, Lakshmi stood before the trader's two goats with her self-help group's money tied in her dupatta. "Eighteen thousand for the pair," the trader said, "and I'm giving you a good rate." Lakshmi felt her mind start to bargain from there: sixteen, maybe fifteen. She stopped. If he hadn't said eighteen, what would she think these goats were worth? She didn't know. "I'll come back," she said. Her friend Sangeeta raised an eyebrow. "He might sell them." "Then he sells them." Together they walked the rows. A man near the banyan tree was asking eleven for a similar pair. Sangeeta's cousin, who kept goats in the next village, said on the phone that ten to twelve was fair this season. Lakshmi went back with her own figure. She bought the pair for twelve.

qa.q: How much did the trader first ask for the pair of goats?
qa.a: Eighteen thousand for the pair.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "I'll come back" even though the goats might be sold?
qa.a: She realised her bargaining was starting from the trader's eighteen, not from any real knowledge. She preferred to risk losing the goats than to spend the group's money on his number.

qa.q: Which step made Lakshmi's final price fair?
qa.a: Getting two separate comparisons, the man near the banyan tree and Sangeeta's cousin, before going back. That gave her a figure that did not depend on the first price.

qa.q: How might the other women in Lakshmi's self-help group feel about how she spent their money?
qa.a: They would likely trust her more, since she saved thousands by checking prices rather than accepting a trader's opening figure.

grounding: At a village market, a young woman stops bargaining from a trader's first price, asks what she would judge without it, and checks two other prices.
